docs.title: markwright
docs.text:
markwright is a set of Python-Markdown extensions plus a companion CLI, mw, for author-friendly markdown: highlighted text, labeled code fences, and media embeds. Use the extensions in any tool built on Python-Markdown (including MkDocs), or the mw pipeline in toolchains that are not, like Hugo.

Part of markwright is a port: the highlight, fence, and media embed extensions reproduce the syntax and HTML output of DigitalOcean's do-markdownit. Everything else is markwright's own: buttons, lightboxes, Mermaid diagrams, icons, grids and cards, annotations, tabs, click-to-load embeds, a config system, and the mw CLI, which runs the same extensions as pre and post filters around any renderer.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Highlight wraps <^>text<^> in <mark>, and works inside inline code and fenced code blocks where ==text== cannot reach.
  • Fence adds labels, secondary labels, environment classes, and command-line prefixes to code blocks.
  • YouTube turns [youtube ID] into a responsive iframe embed.
  • CodePen embeds a pen with theme, default-tab, and layout options.
  • Twitter embeds a tweet with theme and alignment options.
  • Instagram embeds a post with caption and alignment options.
  • Slideshow builds an image slideshow with navigation arrows.
  • Image Compare renders two images with a draggable before/after slider.
  • Button turns [button URL TEXT] into a link styled as a button.
  • Lightbox turns [lightbox URL ALT] into an image link a host script can open in an overlay.
  • Mermaid turns a mermaid code fence into a <pre class="mermaid"> block a host script draws.
  • Icons replaces :pack-name: shortcodes with inline SVG from directories you configure.
  • Grid classes the list after [grid] or [grid cards], wraps the blocks between [grid] and [/grid] as grid cells with [card] ... [/card] cards inside, and sets a 1-to-6 column count with [grid N].
  • Annotate links (N) markers in a code block to the items of the numbered list after it.
  • Tabs groups consecutive [tab NAME] ... [/tab] blocks into one tabbed set.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
uv add markwright

Or install from a local path:

uv add --editable ../markwright

MkDocs 2.0 Compatibility

MkDocs 2.0 removes the plugin system and rewrites the theming architecture, breaking all existing plugins and themes including Material for MkDocs. There is no migration path. This project's dev dependency is mkdocs>=1.6,<2, and its lock file resolves to MkDocs 1.6.1.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
These extensions work with Python-Markdown directly, so you can use them in any Python program (a Flask app, a CLI tool, a static site generator, or a simple script).

import markdown

md = markdown.Markdown(
    extensions=[
        "pymdownx.superfences",
        "pymdownx.highlight",
        "markwright.highlight",
        "markwright.fence",
        "markwright.youtube",
        "markwright.codepen",
        "markwright.twitter",
        "markwright.instagram",
        "markwright.slideshow",
        "markwright.image_compare",
        "markwright.button",
        "markwright.lightbox",
        "markwright.mermaid",
        "markwright.grid",
        "markwright.annotate",
        "markwright.tabs",
    ]
)

source = """
```command
[label deploy.sh]
ssh root@server
apt update
```
"""

html = md.convert(source)
print(html)

You can also load only the extensions you need by listing just those in the extensions list.

Using MkDocs? See Using with MkDocs for the mkdocs.yml configuration.

Note

The fence extension should be used alongside pymdownx.superfences and pymdownx.highlight for proper code block rendering. Without them, the fence preprocessor will still extract directives, but the code block HTML structure may differ from what the postprocessor expects.

docs.title: Using It Outside Python
docs.text:
If your toolchain is not built on Python-Markdown, the mw command-line tool runs the same extensions as pre and post filters around any renderer:

mw pre < in.md | your-renderer | mw post > out.html

See the CLI Reference for the commands and flags, and the Hugo integration guide for a worked setup.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Each extension is a standalone Python-Markdown extension loaded by name (e.g., markwright.highlight). The extensions use these processor patterns:

  1. Fence uses a Preprocessor (priority 40) that runs before pymdownx.superfences to extract directives. A Postprocessor (priority 25) injects labels, classes, and prefix markup into rendered HTML.

  2. Embeds use Preprocessors (priority 20) that run after superfences, matching standalone [name ...] lines. Social embeds add a Postprocessor (priority 15) for one-time script injection.

  3. Highlight uses an InlineProcessor (priority 175) for regular text, plus a Postprocessor (priority 25) for <^> markers inside code blocks where the delimiters are HTML-escaped.

  4. Button, Lightbox, and Mermaid use Preprocessors only. Button and Lightbox (priority 20) match standalone directive lines like the embeds. Mermaid (priority 45) replaces mermaid fences with a raw <pre> before superfences sees them.

  5. Icons uses a pre stage (priority 5, after every directive stage) for mw pre and an InlineProcessor (priority 85) in-process, both resolving :pack-name: shortcodes against SVG directories you configure.

  6. Grid and Annotate follow the fence marker-comment pattern: a Preprocessor (priority 20, or 21 for grid, which runs ahead of Python-Markdown's html_block) swaps the directive for a versioned marker comment, and a Postprocessor (priority 27) reads it from the rendered HTML.

  7. Tabs follow the same marker-comment pattern: a Preprocessor (priority 21) swaps each [tab NAME] ... [/tab] block for a pair of marker comments, and a Postprocessor (priority 27) groups consecutive tabs into one tabbed-set.

markwright ships no CSS, JavaScript, or icons. The extensions emit classes and markup, and the host site styles them.

docs.title: CLI Reference (mw)
docs.text:
The mw command exposes the markwright extensions as Unix filters, so their Markdown syntax works in toolchains that are not built on Python-Markdown. It is a stdin-to-stdout tool: every transform subcommand reads standard input and writes standard output, so it composes in any pipe. Input and output are UTF-8.

The console script ships with the package. After uv add markwright (or pip install markwright), the mw command is on your path.

docs.title: Subcommands
docs.text:
mw pre    [--config PATH] [--exclude NAME]
mw post   [--config PATH] [--exclude NAME] [--warn | --no-warn]
mw render [--config PATH] [--exclude NAME]
mw config [--config PATH] [--exclude NAME]
mw list
mw --version

Which extensions run, and how each is configured, come from a config file. See Configuration for the file format, discovery, and precedence.

docs.title: mw pre
docs.text:
Reads Markdown source and writes Markdown with the source-stage transforms applied. It expands the embed, [button ...], and [lightbox ...] directives into raw HTML, turns mermaid fences into <pre class="mermaid"> blocks, and resolves :pack-name: icon shortcodes to inline SVG. It extracts fence, [grid], [annotate], and [tab NAME] directives into marker comments (<!-- mw-fence:{JSON} --> and its siblings) that the post stage reads back later. It pairs the containers ([grid] ... [/grid] with its [card] ... [/card] cards, and [tab NAME] ... [/tab]) into marker comments the same way, and leaves an unpaired opener or closer literal with a problem marker that mw post --warn reports. With the highlight extension active, it also wraps prose <^>...<^> runs in <mark>, leaving in-code markers for the post stage. A leading YAML (---) or TOML (+++) front matter block passes through untouched. A first line of --- counts as front matter when a later --- line closes it, so start a document that opens with a thematic break with *** or ___.

The output is meant to feed your renderer. Because the expanded embeds and the <mark> wrappers are raw HTML, your renderer must pass raw HTML through. See Renderer Requirements.

docs.title: mw post
docs.text:
Reads rendered HTML and writes HTML with the HTML-stage transforms applied. It styles fence code blocks from their mw-fence markers (label divs, environment classes, <ol><li data-prefix> wrapping), classes grid lists, wraps block grids, cards, and tab sets from their markers, links annotations, wraps any remaining highlight markers in <mark>, and injects each embed script exactly once.

The post stage is the complete path on its own. It needs no marker from the pre stage to inject scripts: it detects each embed's class signature in the rendered HTML, so it also works on hand-authored embeds. Running post twice does not double-inject a script or double-wrap a mark.

docs.title: mw render
docs.text: Runs the full Markdown-to-HTML pipeline in one shot using the in-process Python-Markdown path. This is the standalone renderer for callers who do not have their own. It builds a markdown.Markdown with pymdownx.superfences and pymdownx.highlight plus the selected markwright.* extensions, matching the bundled site stack. It loads no other extension, so tables, admonitions, and the rest of Python-Markdown's and pymdownx's syntax are not available through it. Its syntax highlighting needs Pygments, which markwright does not install; without it code blocks render unhighlighted.

docs.title: mw config
docs.text:
Prints the resolved configuration: each extension's on/off state, the per-extension options, and the warn default, with the source of every value (the built-in default, the config file path, or a CLI flag). It reads the same config discovery and flags a real run would, so it shows exactly what mw pre, mw post, and mw render will use.

$ mw config
extensions:
  youtube: on (default)
  slideshow: on (default)
  image_compare: on (default)
  codepen: on (default)
  twitter: on (default)
  instagram: on (default)
  fence: on (default)
  highlight: on (default)
  button: on (default)
  lightbox: on (default)
  mermaid: on (default)
  icons: on (default)
  grid: on (default)
  annotate: on (default)
  tabs: on (default)
warn: false (default)
load:
  youtube: eager (default)
  codepen: eager (default)
  twitter: eager (default)
  instagram: eager (default)
options: none

docs.title: mw list
docs.text:
Prints every registered extension and the stages it provides.

$ mw list
youtube: pre
slideshow: pre
image_compare: pre
codepen: pre, post
twitter: pre, post
instagram: pre, post
fence: pre, post
highlight: pre, post
button: pre
lightbox: pre
mermaid: pre
icons: pre
grid: pre, post
annotate: pre, post
tabs: pre, post

An extension labeled pre has only a source-stage transform. An extension labeled pre, post participates in both stages.

docs.title: --config PATH
docs.text: Load configuration from PATH, bypassing the walk-up discovery. The file may be a standalone markwright.toml or a pyproject.toml with a [tool.markwright] table. A missing path, or a pyproject.toml with no [tool.markwright] table, is a usage error. Without --config, discovery walks up from the current directory. See Configuration.

docs.title: --exclude NAME
docs.text:
Drop the named extension from the selected set. The flag is repeatable. --exclude applies last, after the config-resolved selection, so you can start from what the config selects and remove a few for one run.

Selection order does not matter. Stages always run in their defined priority order, matching the in-process behavior. An unknown name passed to --exclude (or named in config) is a usage error (see exit codes).

The allowlist that older versions set with --use now lives in config as enable. --use was removed in 0.2.0.

If the selection ends up empty (enable = [], a disable that lists every extension, or --exclude removing the rest), the run still succeeds: pre and post pass their input through unchanged, and render renders plain Markdown with every markwright directive left as literal text. That is useful for switching markwright off inside a longer tool chain, but it is never silent: mw writes one mw: warning: line to stderr naming the cause and the config file, and stdout stays clean for the pipe. An empty fence.allowed_environments warns the same way. Warnings from other libraries keep Python's standard format, so mw: warning: always means markwright's own. See Config Rules.

docs.title: --warn and --no-warn (post only)
docs.text:
--warn turns the diagnostics on and --no-warn turns them off, whatever the warn config key says. When both appear, the last one wins. With neither, the config key decides, and it defaults to off.

The diagnostics are advisory lines on stderr for markers the post stage sees but cannot fully apply. They change no output and do not change the exit code. They are plain stderr lines, not Python warnings, so PYTHONWARNINGS=error does not escalate them.

They report the conditions a post-only filter can detect, for the mw-fence, mw-grid, mw-annotate, and mw-tab markers and the others the pre stage writes (see Renderer Requirements):

  • A malformed JSON payload, which is skipped rather than executed.
  • A marker whose version this tool does not support.
  • A marker with nothing to apply to, such as a fence marker with no code block after it or an annotate marker with no block after it.
  • An open marker with no matching close marker, or the reverse.
  • A grid or tab directive the pre stage left literal because it had no partner or no grid around it (an unclosed [card], a stray [/tab], a [card] outside a grid).

With the diagnostics off, each of these is a silent no-op. A renderer that strips a marker comment outright is undetectable here, since the marker is simply gone; that case is covered by the renderer requirements, not by runtime detection.

docs.title: --version
docs.text: Prints the installed package version and exits.

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text:
• 0 on success, including a run with no extensions selected (which warns on stderr).
  • 2 on a usage error: an unknown subcommand, an unknown name passed to --exclude, or a config problem (a missing, unreadable, non-UTF-8, or malformed file, an unknown extension or option, or a bad value). A config problem, or, for mw pre, mw post, and mw render, input that is not UTF-8, a closed stdout, a broken pipe, or an icon file that cannot be read, prints one mw: error: line on stderr; argparse reports its own usage errors. mw list and mw config write with plain print, so a broken pipe on them is not covered by that rule. A ConfigWarning escalated with PYTHONWARNINGS=error mw ... also exits 2 with an mw: error: line.

docs.title: The Canonical Pipeline
docs.text:
Bracket any renderer with the two stages:

mw pre < in.md | some-renderer | mw post > out.html

The pre stage prepares the source, your renderer turns Markdown into HTML, and the post stage applies the HTML-level styling and script injection. To select a subset of features, set enable (or disable) in a config file both stages discover, or pass the same --exclude flags to both:

mw pre --exclude codepen < in.md | some-renderer | mw post --exclude codepen > out.html

For the full integration model, including when to run only the post stage, see the Pipeline Guide.

docs.title: Click-to-Load
docs.text:
The YouTube, CodePen, Twitter, and Instagram embeds contact a third party. With the default load = "eager", that happens on page load: the provider sets cookies, a strict Content-Security-Policy blocks it, and an offline reader sees empty boxes.

load = "click" replaces the live embed with an inert preview. The live markup still ships in the page, inside a <template>, which browsers parse but never render or fetch from. Nothing reaches the provider until a reader clicks the button and a host script swaps the live markup in.

markwright ships no JavaScript and no CSS. It owns the markup; your site owns the behavior and the styling. This page is the contract a host script codes against.

docs.title: Turning It On
docs.text:
Set load per embed in markwright.toml (or [tool.markwright], or a host tool's own config through config_from_mapping):

[youtube]
load = "click"

[twitter]
load = "click"

In-process, pass it through extension_configs:

md = markdown.Markdown(
    extensions=["markwright.youtube"],
    extension_configs={"markwright.youtube": {"load": "click"}},
)

YouTube also takes load = "lazy", which keeps the live iframe and adds the browser-native loading="lazy". The script embeds take only eager and click, since deferring a script embed needs host JavaScript either way, and click already covers that.

docs.title: The Preview Markup (Version 1)
docs.text:
A [twitter MattIPv4/status/1576415168426573825] line with load = "click" renders to:

<div class="mw-embed" data-mw-version="1" data-mw-embed="twitter" data-mw-load="click" data-mw-script="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js">
    <template class="mw-embed-content"><div class="twitter">
    <blockquote class="twitter-tweet" data-dnt="true" data-width="550" data-theme="light">
        <a href="https://twitter.com/MattIPv4/status/1576415168426573825">View tweet by @MattIPv4</a>
    </blockquote>
</div></template>
    <div class="mw-embed-preview">
        <p class="mw-embed-provider">X (Twitter) post</p>
        <button type="button" class="mw-embed-load">Load post</button>
        <a class="mw-embed-link" href="https://twitter.com/MattIPv4/status/1576415168426573825">View on X</a>
    </div>
</div>

The <template> holds the exact eager markup, minus the provider <script> tag.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Hook Meaning .mw-embed The wrapper; replace it with the live markup on load. data-mw-version The contract version, 1 today. data-mw-embed The extension name: youtube, codepen, twitter, or instagram. data-mw-load The load mode, click. data-mw-script The provider script to inject after cloning. Absent for YouTube, whose iframe needs no script. template.mw-embed-content The live markup. .mw-embed-preview The visible placeholder; style it however your site likes. .mw-embed-provider Text naming what the embed is. button.mw-embed-load The load button. a.mw-embed-link A direct link to the original, so the content stays reachable with JavaScript off and in feed readers.

docs.title: Preview Text
docs.text:
Embed Provider text Button Link youtube YouTube video Load video Watch on YouTube codepen CodePen Load pen View on CodePen twitter X (Twitter) post Load post View on X instagram Instagram post Load post View on Instagram

The text is fixed English. A site that translates it rewrites the text through the hooks above.

docs.title: Script Injection
docs.text: On an eager page, markwright appends each provider's <script> once. It skips the script when every embed of that kind on the page is a preview, and still appends it once when the page mixes eager and click embeds. The decision comes from the HTML alone, so mw post and the in-process render agree.

docs.title: Provider Processors
docs.text:
After cloning the live markup into the page, a host has to make the provider render it:

Embed After the script loads twitter window.twttr.widgets.load(element) renders the tweets inside element (the whole document.body when called with no argument). instagram window.instgrm.Embeds.process() renders every unprocessed post on the page. codepen ei.js scans the page once when it loads. For later embeds, call window.__CPEmbed(), which takes an optional CSS selector (default .codepen) and replaces each match with an iframe, so a repeat call never renders a pen twice. youtube Nothing; the iframe loads itself.

These calls were checked against the providers' live scripts on 2026-10-11 (widgets.js, embed.js, and ei.js).

docs.title: Versioning Policy
docs.text: data-mw-version changes only for a breaking change to the markup above (a renamed hook, a moved element). Adding a hook or an attribute keeps the version.

docs.title: A Host Script
docs.text:
This is a starting point, not package data: copy it into your site and adjust it.

<script>
document.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const button = event.target.closest(".mw-embed-load");
  if (!button) return;
  const wrapper = button.closest(".mw-embed");
  const live = document.createElement("div");
  live.className = "mw-embed-live";
  live.append(wrapper.querySelector("template.mw-embed-content").content.cloneNode(true));
  wrapper.replaceWith(live);

  const scriptSrc = wrapper.dataset.mwScript;
  if (!scriptSrc) return;
  const process = () => {
    const embed = wrapper.dataset.mwEmbed;
    if (embed === "twitter") window.twttr?.widgets?.load(live);
    if (embed === "instagram") window.instgrm?.Embeds?.process();
    if (embed === "codepen") window.__CPEmbed?.();
  };
  if (document.querySelector(`script[src="${scriptSrc}"]`)) {
    process();
    return;
  }
  const script = document.createElement("script");
  script.src = scriptSrc;
  script.async = true;
  script.onload = process;
  document.body.append(script);
});
</script>

One listener on document handles every preview on the page, including ones added later. The script loads each provider at most once; a second click on the same kind of embed reuses it.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: markwright reads a config file to decide which extensions run and how each one is tuned. The file is the durable, primary tuning surface; the CLI flags are thin per-run overrides. The default, with no config and no flags, is every extension on.

docs.title: File Names
docs.text:
markwright looks for two files, in this order within a directory:

  1. A standalone markwright.toml.
  2. A pyproject.toml with a [tool.markwright] table.

If both exist in the same directory, markwright.toml wins (matching how ruff resolves its own config). In a standalone markwright.toml, the settings are top-level tables and keys. In pyproject.toml, the same settings live under [tool.markwright] (so an extension table is [tool.markwright.fence]).

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Without --config, markwright discovers the file by walking up from the current directory to the filesystem root. The first directory that has a markwright.toml, or a pyproject.toml with a [tool.markwright] table, wins; the search stops there. This is the same walk-up model ruff and other tools use, so a config at your project root applies to a run started from any subdirectory.

--config PATH bypasses discovery and loads exactly that file. A missing path, or a pyproject.toml with no [tool.markwright] table, is an error.

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
Three layers resolve each run, highest priority first:

  1. A CLI flag (--exclude, and --warn or --no-warn on mw post).
  2. The project config file (markwright.toml, else [tool.markwright]).
  3. The built-in default (all extensions on, no per-extension options, warn off).

Run mw config to print the resolved result and the source of every value.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text: The recognized top-level keys are enable, disable, warn, and one table per extension.

docs.title: enable and disable
docs.text:
Both are lists of extension names, and they are mutually exclusive: setting both is an error.

  • enable = ["fence", "youtube"] runs only those two.
  • enable = [] runs no extensions and emits a warning (see Config Rules).
  • disable = ["codepen"] runs every extension except that one.
  • Neither key runs every extension (the default).

The valid names are fence, highlight, youtube, codepen, twitter, instagram, slideshow, image_compare, button, lightbox, mermaid, icons, grid, annotate, and tabs. An unknown name is an error.

docs.title: warn
docs.text: A boolean default for the mw post stage's marker diagnostics. It defaults to false.

docs.title: Per-Extension Options
docs.text:
Each extension may take an options table named for it. Config validates every key and value with the same reader the extension uses, so an option the extension does not take, or a bad value, is an error before anything renders. The fence extension reads allowed_environments, a list restricting which [environment ...] directives are honored. Omitting it allows every environment; an empty list allows none and emits a warning.

It also reads label_class and secondary_label_class, the CSS classes on the label <div> and the secondary label <div>. They default to code-label and secondary-code-label. Each is one or more space-separated class tokens of letters, digits, -, and _; an empty value, a non-string, or any other character is a ConfigError.

[fence]
allowed_environments = ["local", "staging", "production"]
label_class = "code-label"
secondary_label_class = "secondary-code-label"

The embeds that contact a third party (youtube, codepen, twitter, instagram) read load, which decides when the embed reaches out.

Value Extensions Output eager (default) all four The live embed, unchanged from earlier releases. lazy youtube only The iframe gets loading="lazy", so the browser fetches it when it scrolls near the viewport. click all four An inert preview with a load button; nothing loads until a host script swaps in the live embed. 
[youtube]
load = "click"

[twitter]
load = "click"

Config validation checks load: an unsupported value, or load on an extension that does not take it, is an error. See Click-to-Load for the preview markup and a host script.

The icons extension reads packs, a table that maps a shortcode prefix to a directory of SVG files. markwright ships no icons, so with packs omitted the extension does nothing and :pack-name: shortcodes pass through unchanged.

[icons.packs]
lucide = "docs/icons/lucide"
mw = "docs/icons/mw"

An empty packs table is a no-op and emits a ConfigWarning. A packs value that is not a table, a path that is not a string, or a directory that does not exist is a ConfigError. Relative directories resolve against the directory you run from. See Icons.

An unknown top-level key, or a table named for an extension that does not exist, is an error. This catches typos rather than ignoring them.

docs.title: Config Rules
docs.text:
These rules hold for every markwright setting, including any added later.

  1. Omitting a key means its default. For a list, the default is no restriction. A key set to null (a YAML key with no value, from a host tool's config) counts as omitted.
  2. A list names exactly what it holds. An empty allowlist (enable, fence.allowed_environments) allows nothing. An empty denylist (disable) removes nothing. No list treats empty as "everything".
  3. A setting that turns a feature into a no-op is legal and never silent. It emits a markwright.ConfigWarning naming the key and, when markwright loaded the config, its source. mw prints it as one mw: warning: line on stderr and keeps stdout clean; a host sees a standard Python warning it can filter or escalate. Python's default filter shows a given warning message once per call site, so a site that builds one Markdown per page prints it once per build. Filtering Python warnings (PYTHONWARNINGS=ignore) silences it; escalating them (python -W error) turns it into an error, which mw reports as mw: error: with exit code 2. MkDocs routes Python warnings into its log, so there it appears as a log line, and mkdocs build --strict does not fail on it.
  4. Every option markwright defines is validated, and only those are accepted. An unknown option key, a wrong type, or an unsupported value is a ConfigError naming the extension, the key, and the source, never a fallback or a traceback. The Python-Markdown path raises markwright.OptionError (a ValueError subclass) for the same bad values.

Rule 3 is why an empty selection does not error: switching markwright off is useful when testing a longer tool chain, but it should never happen by accident without a trace.

docs.title: A Standalone markwright.toml
docs.text:
# Run every extension except CodePen, and restrict fence environments.
disable = ["codepen"]

[fence]
allowed_environments = ["local", "staging", "production"]

docs.title: The Same Config in pyproject.toml
docs.text:
[tool.markwright]
disable = ["codepen"]

[tool.markwright.fence]
allowed_environments = ["local", "staging", "production"]

docs.title: A Hugo Pipeline
docs.text:
A Hugo site runs mw pre on its content, then hugo, then mw post on the rendered pages. Both stages discover the same markwright.toml at the project root, so a single file configures the whole pipeline. With the fence allowed_environments set as above, mw pre honors an [environment staging] directive and rejects an unlisted one, exactly as the in-process mw render does.

mw pre < content/post.md > content/post.md.tmp && mv content/post.md.tmp content/post.md
hugo
mw post < public/post/index.html > public/post/index.html.tmp && mv public/post/index.html.tmp public/post/index.html

See the Hugo guide for the hugo.toml settings and a script that does this for every file.

Because the options come from the config file both stages read, you set them once and both the pre and post stages agree.

docs.title: Using markwright Config from Another Tool
docs.text:
A host tool (a static site generator, for example) can carry a markwright table inside its own config file and get the same validation markwright.toml gets. The host parses its own file, then hands markwright the table:

from pathlib import Path

import markdown
import yaml

from markwright import ConfigError, config_from_mapping, extension_configs, selected_extensions

host_config = yaml.safe_load(Path("bartleby.yml").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

try:
    config = config_from_mapping(host_config.get("markwright", {}), source="bartleby.yml: markwright")
except ConfigError as config_error:
    raise SystemExit(str(config_error)) from config_error

names = selected_extensions(config)
md = markdown.Markdown(
    extensions=[f"markwright.{name}" for name in names],
    extension_configs=extension_configs(config, names),
)
  • config_from_mapping(table, source) validates the table with the same rules as a config file and returns a Config. Every error message starts with the source label, and no file discovery happens. A table that is not a mapping is a ConfigError, None reads as an empty table, and an unknown key is an error whatever its value, None included.
  • selected_extensions(config) applies enable and disable and returns extension names in registry order.
  • extension_configs(config, names) returns the per-extension option tables keyed markwright.<name>, ready for markdown.Markdown.
  • disallowed_environments(source, config) returns the fence environment names a document uses outside fence.allowed_environments, each once, in order of first appearance. A name is everything after the first space of the [environment NAME] line, compared as written. Every disallowed environment line among a fence's leading lines is reported, although mw pre stops reading directives at the first one, and a directive inside a nested fence's source is code. A mermaid fence is skipped when mermaid is selected and scanned when it is excluded. The list is empty when allowed_environments is omitted or fence is not selected, and an empty allowlist reports every name. It emits no warning of its own, so printing the result is the host's decision.

mw render builds its own markdown.Markdown from selected_extensions and extension_configs, so a host and the CLI resolve a given table the same way.

When a config selects no extensions, selected_extensions returns an empty list and emits a markwright.ConfigWarning with the cause and the source label. It does not raise, since an empty selection is a legitimate way to switch markwright off. A host that wants it fatal (in its own test suite, say) can escalate it:

import warnings

from markwright import ConfigWarning

warnings.simplefilter("error", ConfigWarning)

docs.title: Material Mapping
docs.text:
This page answers one question: you use a feature from the Material for MkDocs reference, and you want to know what provides it in-process and what provides it under Hugo. In-process means Python-Markdown, with or without MkDocs. Under Hugo means Goldmark and Chroma, with markwright's mw pre and mw post filters around the build (see the Hugo guide).

The in-process column follows this site's mkdocs.yml. The Hugo column was checked with a pipeline build on a small Hugo site using the settings from the Hugo guide. Where a cell says "no equivalent", markwright and Hugo give you nothing for that feature, and the gap is yours to fill. markwright emits classes and markup only and ships no CSS, JavaScript, or icons, so a row that needs styling or a script depends on your host; this site's docs/ folder is the worked example.

docs.title: Pipeline Guide
docs.text:
The mw CLI lets you use markwright syntax in a toolchain that is not built on Python-Markdown. It brackets your existing renderer with two filters: a pre stage that runs on Markdown source, and a post stage that runs on the rendered HTML. This page covers the model and shows worked Hugo and plain-Unix examples.

For the per-flag reference, see the CLI Reference.

docs.title: The Pre / Render / Post Model
docs.text:
Every markwright feature decomposes into at most two pure string transforms. A source-stage transform takes Markdown text and returns Markdown with embedded HTML and marker comments. An HTML-stage transform takes rendered HTML and returns rendered HTML. Your renderer runs between them.

flowchart LR
    A[Markdown source] --> B[mw pre]
    B --> C[your renderer]
    C --> D[mw post]
    D --> E[final HTML]

The pre stage expands the embed, button, lightbox, mermaid, and icon directives into raw HTML, resolves prose highlights, and turns the fence, grid, card, annotate, and tab directives into marker comments (see Renderer Requirements). Your renderer turns Markdown into HTML, passing the raw HTML and the comments through. The post stage reads the marker comments back to apply fence labels and prefixes, grid, card, and tab markup, and annotation links, and it resolves the remaining highlight markers and injects one-time embed scripts.

docs.title: When to Run Only Post
docs.text:
You do not always need both stages.

Run both stages when your source contains pre-stage syntax: embed, button, and lightbox directives like [youtube ID], mermaid fences and icon shortcodes, or directives that leave a marker for the post stage, like [label deploy.sh], [grid], [annotate], and [tab NAME]. The pre stage has to expand those before your renderer sees them.

Run only the post stage when your HTML already carries the embed markup and any highlight markers, and you want the post-stage styling and script injection. The post stage detects each embed's class signature on its own, so it injects scripts for hand-authored embeds with no pre-stage marker. Highlight is also complete in the post stage: after a render, both prose and in-code markers surface as escaped text, and a single post pass handles both.

Run only the pre stage when you want prose highlights resolved to <mark> before your renderer runs, and nothing else.

The two stages are safe to combine. Pre resolves prose highlights, post resolves whatever markers remain, and running post twice changes nothing.

docs.title: Plain Unix Example
docs.text:
The shortest path is a single pipe:

mw pre < in.md | cmark --unsafe | mw post > out.html

cmark --unsafe is CommonMark with raw-HTML passthrough enabled, which the expanded embeds require. To run a subset, pass matching flags to both stages:

mw pre --exclude twitter --exclude instagram < in.md \
  | cmark --unsafe \
  | mw post --exclude twitter --exclude instagram > out.html

If your source has no other directives and you only want highlight styling, restrict the run to that extension. Set it once in a config file both stages discover:

# markwright.toml
enable = ["highlight"]

cmark --unsafe < in.md | mw post > out.html

See Configuration for the file format and precedence.

docs.title: Hugo
docs.text: Hugo is a worked, tested instance of this model, with Goldmark as the renderer. See the Hugo integration guide for the exact hugo.toml settings and a build script that brackets a real site.

docs.title: Renderer Requirements
docs.text: The mw pre and mw post stages coordinate through markers that survive a normal Markdown render, not through any knowledge of the renderer. For that round-trip to work, the renderer you place between the two stages has to meet three requirements. Each requirement maps to a feature, and a renderer that does not meet one disables that feature while leaving the rest working.

docs.title: 1. Raw HTML Passthrough
docs.text: The pre stage expands embed, button, and lightbox directives into raw HTML, turns mermaid fences into a <pre> block, inlines icon SVG, and, with highlight active, wraps prose markers in <mark>. A renderer that strips raw HTML by default has to enable its passthrough option (--unsafe for cmark, unsafe = true for Hugo's Goldmark, and the equivalent elsewhere). Without passthrough, the expanded HTML and pre-stage highlights are dropped by the renderer before the post stage ever sees them.

docs.title: 2. Comment Preservation
docs.text: The pre stage encodes the fence, grid, annotate, and tabs directives as HTML comments (listed under Marker Comments) and the post stage reads them back. For a fence, the <!-- mw-fence:{JSON} --> comment sits immediately before the fence, and the post stage uses it to style the adjacent code block. A renderer that preserves HTML comments lets all of these round-trip. A renderer that drops comments disables those four features and breaks nothing else: a code block still renders, just without its label, environment tint, or line prefixes, and a grid, annotation, or tab directive does nothing.

docs.title: 3. Span-Based Syntax Highlighting
docs.text: In-code highlighting (<^>...<^> inside a fence) depends on the renderer wrapping syntax-highlighted tokens in tags, so the post stage can place <mark> without crossing a token boundary. Any Pygments- or Chroma-style highlighter qualifies. A renderer that emits plain, untagged code text still highlights, but the <mark> placement has fewer token boundaries to respect.

docs.title: Marker Comments
docs.text:
Four extensions carry data from the pre stage to the post stage in versioned HTML comments. Each is a public contract, read fail-soft, and each has its payload documented on its own page.

Marker Extension Role mw-fence Fence Carries the fence directives to the code block that follows. mw-grid Grid Classes the list that follows a [grid] or [grid cards] shortcut. mw-grid-block, mw-grid-end Grid Open and close a block grid. mw-card, mw-card-end Grid Open and close a card inside a block grid. mw-annotate Annotate Links the (N) markers in the block that follows to the numbered list after it. mw-tab, mw-tab-end Tabs Open and close one tab, grouped into sets. mw-grid-problem, mw-tab-problem Grid, Tabs Sit after a directive the pre stage left literal, so mw post --warn can report it.

The post stage removes every one of them from its output. The rest of this page describes mw-fence in detail; the others follow the same versioning policy.

docs.title: The mw-fence Marker Contract
docs.text:
The fence directives travel from pre to post as a single HTML comment immediately before the fence:

<!-- mw-fence:{"version": 1, "label": "deploy.sh"} -->

The fence itself is left intact, so your renderer still syntax-highlights the real code. There is no placeholder and no rewritten language token. The post stage associates a marker with the first code block that follows it, before the next marker. For an indented fence (up to three spaces, or inside a list item), the comment carries the fence's indentation and is followed by a blank line, so it stays inside the list item and renders as its own block. This comment is a cross-tool surface, so its shape is a versioned contract.

docs.title: v1 Payload
docs.text:
{
  "version": 1,
  "label": "deploy.sh",
  "secondary_label": "optional second label",
  "environment": "local",
  "prefix_type": "command",
  "prefix_value": "$"
}

version is an integer and the only required field. Every other field is optional and present only when the author used that directive. prefix_type is one of line_numbers, command, super_user, or custom_prefix. prefix_value carries the rendered prefix ($, #, or custom text) and is absent for line_numbers. The post stage applies whatever fields are present and ignores any it does not recognize.

docs.title: Versioning Policy
docs.text:
The policy is best-effort, backward compatible, and fail-soft.

The schema grows additively: a new optional field does not bump version, and only a breaking change does. The post stage reads any marker whose version it knows (currently only 1) and ignores unknown fields, so a newer pre stage that only added fields still works with an older post stage. A marker whose version is greater than the post stage knows is skipped as a no-op and reported under --warn. A malformed payload is skipped, never executed, and reported under --warn: invalid JSON, a payload that is not a JSON object, or a known field of the wrong type (for example a numeric label, or a prefix_type outside the four values). A marker with no code block before the next marker is skipped the same way.

docs.title: What Degrades, and How
docs.text:
The post stage degrades gracefully. If a marker or signature is absent, the matching feature is a no-op rather than an error.

Unmet Requirement Feature That Stops Behavior Raw HTML passthrough Embeds, buttons, lightboxes, mermaid, icons, pre-stage prose highlight The renderer drops the expanded HTML before post runs Comment preservation Fence labels, environments, prefixes; grids, annotations, and tabs Code blocks render unstyled and the other directives do nothing; the skip is silent Span-based highlighting In-code highlight Markers still wrap, with fewer token boundaries to respect

The comment-stripping case is special. Once a renderer drops a marker comment, the post stage has no evidence the directive ever existed, so a stripped marker is silently absent rather than a detectable skip. That is why --warn cannot report it: a post-only filter sees nothing to warn about. Embed script injection is unaffected, since it keys on the embed class signature in the HTML, not on any comment.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Put [annotate] on its own line before a block, write (N) in the block, and follow the block with an ordered list:

[annotate]

```python
name = "markwright"  # (1)
debug = False  # (2)!
```

1. The package name.
2. Switches off debug output.
Marker Result (N) Replaced by a link to list item N. (N)! In a code comment, the whole comment is replaced by the link, so the comment text does not show. A comment that holds several markers, one of them with the !, is replaced by all their links in order. Under Hugo this needs noClasses = false: the comment is found by its highlighter class, and a comment span with only inline styles keeps its # and gets just the link.

A number outside 1 to the item count is left as written, except that it goes with the comment when a valid ! marker replaces that comment, as (9) does in # (1)! (9). Only text counts: a (N) inside an attribute, a <script>, or a <style> is never touched.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Annotate is a two-stage extension. The source stage (mw pre) replaces [annotate] with an <!-- mw-annotate:... --> marker comment. The HTML stage (mw post) finds the block after the marker and the <ol> after the block. It then:

  1. Adds mw-annotated to the block.
  2. Adds mw-annotations and data-mw-version="1" to the list.
  3. Gives each top-level list item an id of the form mw-annotation-B-N, where B counts annotated blocks on the page and N is the item number.
  4. Replaces each marker with <a class="mw-annotation" href="#mw-annotation-B-N">N</a>.

A marker with an invalid payload, no following block, or no ordered list after the block is skipped, and --warn reports why. In-process, annotate's postprocessor (priority 27) runs ahead of fence's (25), so it still sees the fence marker as a comment.

<span class="n">y</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">2</span>  <a class="mw-annotation" href="#mw-annotation-1-2">2</a>
</code></pre></div>
<ol class="mw-annotations" data-mw-version="1">
<li id="mw-annotation-1-1">First</li>
<li id="mw-annotation-1-2">Second</li>

The mw-annotation link class, the mw-annotated and mw-annotations classes, and the mw-annotation-B-N id scheme are the public contract.

A marker with an invalid payload, no following block, or no ordered list after the block is skipped and reported by mw post --warn. The post stage removes the comment from its output.

To put markers in a list's own items, wrap the list in <div markdown>:

[annotate]

<div markdown>

- Write the source (1)
- Render it (2)

1. Plain Markdown with markwright syntax.

The wrapper is for Python-Markdown. It merges any list into a list directly before it, bullet or numbered, so without the </div> the annotation items become more items of the annotated list and annotate finds no annotation list. The markdown attribute needs the md_in_html extension, which mw render does not load, so this form needs a Python-Markdown setup that does (this site's mkdocs.yml does). CommonMark renderers such as Hugo start a new list when the list type changes, so through mw pre | hugo | mw post the wrapper is not needed.

The same merge applies to an annotation list followed directly by a bullet list: put a paragraph between them.

docs.title: Host CSS and Script
docs.text:
markwright ships no CSS, JavaScript, or icons. The hooks are the a.mw-annotation markers that link to #mw-annotation-B-N, the ol.mw-annotations list (tagged data-mw-version="1"), the mw-annotated class added to the annotated block itself (the <p> or whatever block follows the directive), and the mw-annotation-B-N ids on the list items. With no script, each marker is a plain link that jumps to its list item. This site styles annotations after mkdocs-material's:

  • docs/javascripts/annotate.js moves each list item's content into a tooltip card and hides the list. Hovering, focusing, or tapping a marker opens its card, and the card stays open while the pointer is over it. A marker inside a card opens a second card on top, which is what makes nested annotations work. A click pins a card until the next click outside it, and Escape closes every card. Printing puts the content back in the list.
  • docs/stylesheets/extra.css draws the marker as a pulsing circled plus that turns into a cross while its card is open, and slides the card in. The marker's number stays in the link text, hidden on screen, so screen readers announce it and print shows it. Motion is off under prefers-reduced-motion.

To copy the setup into your own MkDocs site, add both files to extra_javascript and extra_css, and enable attr_list and md_in_html if you annotate lists.

docs.text:
The load option decides when the embed contacts the provider. Set it in markwright.toml, or pass it through extension_configs in-process.

Value Output eager (default) The live embed, with the provider script injected once per page. click An inert preview with a load button and a direct link; no provider script. 
[codepen]
load = "click"

md = markdown.Markdown(
    extensions=["markwright.codepen"],
    extension_configs={"markwright.codepen": {"load": "click"}},
)

The load option is separate from the lazy flag above. The flag is CodePen's own preview mode, which still loads the CodePen script; load = "click" loads nothing from CodePen until the reader asks.

See Click-to-Load for the preview markup and a host script that swaps in the live embed.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The embed must be on its own line, with a blank line before and after it; without them the renderer folds the embed into the surrounding paragraph
  • The CodePen embed script is injected once, even with multiple embeds on a page, and only when at least one embed is eager

docs.title: HTML Contract
docs.text:
<p class="codepen" data-height="256" data-theme-id="light" data-default-tab="result" data-user="MattCowley" data-slug-hash="vwPzeX" style="height: 256px; box-sizing: border-box; display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; border: 2px solid; margin: 1em 0; padding: 1em;">
    <span>See the Pen <a href="https://codepen.io/MattCowley/pen/vwPzeX">vwPzeX by MattCowley</a> (<a href="https://codepen.io/MattCowley">@MattCowley</a>) on <a href='https://codepen.io'>CodePen</a>.</span>
</p>

<script async defer src="https://static.codepen.io/assets/embed/ei.js" type="text/javascript"></script>

This is the eager output. The <script> is appended once, at the end of the page.

docs.title: Host CSS and Script
docs.text:
markwright ships no CSS, JavaScript, or icons. In eager mode the embed is a <p class="codepen"> carrying CodePen's data-* attributes (do-markdownit's own CodePen shape), and markwright injects CodePen's <script> once per page, so the host needs no code: CodePen's script renders the pen. This site ships no CodePen rule in docs/stylesheets/extra.css; the pen draws itself.

In click mode the embed is the mw-embed preview instead, whose hooks (.mw-embed, template.mw-embed-content, button.mw-embed-load, and the rest) a host script swaps for the live pen. Click-to-Load is the contract for that markup and carries a worked host script.

docs.title: Fence
docs.text:
Adds labels, secondary labels, environment classes, and line prefixes to fenced code blocks. All fence features are coordinated through a single extension to avoid ordering issues.

server.sh 
Output
  1. ssh root@192.168.1.1

  2. apt update && apt upgrade -y
Markdown 
```command
[environment local]
[label server.sh]
[secondary_label Output]
ssh root@192.168.1.1
apt update && apt upgrade -y
```

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Load markwright.fence alongside pymdownx.superfences and pymdownx.highlight; the fence postprocessor rewrites the code-block HTML those produce.

import markdown

md = markdown.Markdown(
    extensions=[
        "pymdownx.superfences",
        "pymdownx.highlight",
        "markwright.fence",
    ],
    extension_configs={
        "markwright.fence": {
            "allowed_environments": ["local", "second", "third", "fourth", "fifth"],
        },
    },
)
Option Default Description allowed_environments omitted (allow all) List of allowed environment names. Omit it to allow every name; an empty list allows none and emits a ConfigWarning. label_class code-label CSS class for the label div. secondary_label_class secondary-code-label CSS class for the secondary label div.

All three options apply the same way in-process, through mw render, and through the mw pre | renderer | mw post pipeline.

Directives work in any fenced code block CommonMark recognizes, including a fence indented up to three spaces or one nested inside a list item. An unclosed fence is not a code block, so its directives are left as text.

See Using with MkDocs to load it in a MkDocs site.

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
Add a label above a code block with [label TEXT] as the first line inside the fence:

```python
[label app.py]
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)
```
app.py 
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

docs.title: Secondary Labels
docs.text:
Add a secondary label inside the code block with [secondary_label TEXT]:

```
[secondary_label Output]
Hello, world!
```

OutputHello, world!

docs.title: Both Labels Together
docs.text:
```python
[label app.py]
[secondary_label Output]
Hello from Flask!
```
app.py 
OutputHello from Flask!

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
Tint the whole code block with a color using [environment NAME] inside the fence. This helps distinguish code blocks for different server environments:

```
[environment local]
ssh user@local-server
```

ssh user@local-server

```
[environment second]
ssh user@staging-server
```

ssh user@staging-server

```
[environment third]
ssh user@production-server
```

ssh user@production-server

docs.title: Line Prefixes
docs.text: Prefix flags go in the info string (after the backticks). They wrap each code line in <ol><li> with a data-prefix attribute.

docs.title: Line Numbers
docs.text:
```line_numbers,python
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/")
def hello():
    return "Hello!"
```

  1. from flask import Flask

  2. 

  3. app = Flask(__name__)

  4. 

  5. @app.route("/")

  6. def hello():

  7.     return "Hello!"

docs.title: Command Prefix ($)
docs.text:
Implicitly sets the language to bash:

```command
sudo apt update
sudo apt install nginx
```

  1. sudo apt update

  2. sudo apt install nginx

docs.title: Super User Prefix (#)
docs.text:
Implicitly sets the language to bash:

```super_user
systemctl restart nginx
```

  1. systemctl restart nginx

docs.title: Custom Prefix
docs.text:
Implicitly sets the language to bash. Use \s for spaces:

```custom_prefix(mysql>)
SELECT * FROM users;
SHOW TABLES;
```

  1. SELECT * FROM users;

  2. SHOW TABLES;

docs.title: HTML Contract
docs.text:
A label is a <div class="code-label"> before the highlighted block, and a secondary label is a <div class="secondary-code-label"> inside its <code> element:

<div class="code-label" title="app.py">app.py</div>

<div class="language-python highlight"><pre><span></span><code><div class="secondary-code-label" title="Output">Output</div>...</code></pre></div>

An environment and a line prefix add classes to the <pre> and wrap each line in an <ol><li data-prefix="...">:

<div class="code-label" title="deploy.sh">deploy.sh</div>

<div class="language-bash highlight"><pre class="prefixed command environment-local"><span></span><code><ol><li data-prefix="$">ls
</li></ol>
</code></pre></div>

The <pre> class is prefixed plus the prefix type (line_numbers, command, super_user, or custom_prefix), and environment-NAME when an environment is set. data-prefix is $, #, the custom text, or the line number.

docs.title: Host CSS and Script
docs.text:
markwright ships no CSS, JavaScript, or icons. The fence extension emits these hooks:

Hook Where Role div.code-label Before the block The label chip, with a title. The class is the label_class option's default. div.secondary-code-label Inside the <code> The secondary label. The class is the secondary_label_class option's default. pre.environment-NAME On the <pre> The environment tint, where NAME is the sanitized [environment NAME] value. pre.prefixed <type> On the <pre> A line-prefixed block, where <type> is line_numbers, command, super_user, or custom_prefix. <ol><li data-prefix="..."> Inside the <code> One list item per line, each carrying its prefix string.

No host script is involved; the block works as plain highlighted code, and the hooks only change how it looks. This site draws the label chips, tints the five demo environments, and renders each line's data-prefix through a CSS ::before in docs/stylesheets/extra.css, under the .code-label, pre.environment-*, and pre.prefixed rules. A host that renames the label classes through the options styles its own names instead.

docs.title: Grid
docs.text:
Lays content out in a grid. A [grid ...] line classes the list after it, and a paired [grid ...] and [/grid] wrap any blocks between them in a grid <div>, with [card] and [/card] grouping those blocks into cards.

Mark Text

Highlight a word in prose, in inline code, or inside a code block.

Highlight

Label Code

Add labels, environments, and $ or # prompts to fenced code.

Fence

Explain Code

Link (1) markers in a block to notes that open as tooltips.

Annotate

Markdown 
[grid cards 3]

[card]

**Mark Text**

Highlight a word in prose, in inline code, or inside a code block.

[Highlight](highlight.md)

[/card]

[card]

**Label Code**

Add labels, environments, and `$` or `#` prompts to fenced code.

[Fence](fence.md)

[/card]

[card]

**Explain Code**

Link `(1)` markers in a block to notes that open as tooltips.

[Annotate](annotate.md)

[/card]

[/grid]

The directive lines are inside the source fence above, so the pre stage leaves them literal and the fence renders the source as written.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import markdown

md = markdown.Markdown(extensions=["markwright.grid"])

See Using with MkDocs to load it in a MkDocs site.

docs.title: Grid Shortcut
docs.text:
A [grid ...] line with no closer is the list shortcut. It classes the first <ul> or <ol> that follows it. The directive is on its own line, with a blank line before the list.

  • Mark: highlight a word in prose or code.
  • Label: add a label and a prompt to a fence.
  • Explain: link a marker to a note.
Markdown 
[grid cards]

- **Mark**: highlight a word in prose or code.
- **Label**: add a label and a prompt to a fence.
- **Explain**: link a marker to a note.
Directive Result [grid] The next list gets class="mw-grid". [grid cards] The next list gets class="mw-grid mw-grid-cards".

docs.title: Column Counts
docs.text:
Add a count from 1 to 6 to pin the number of columns. The token order is free, so [grid 3], [grid cards 3], and [grid 3 cards] are all the same. Any other token, a second count, a count outside 1 to 6, or a repeated flag leaves the line literal.

A count adds mw-grid-cols-N to the grid. Without one, this site's sample flows into as many columns as fit and drops to one on a narrow screen.

Directive Classes [grid 3] mw-grid mw-grid-cols-3 [grid cards 3] mw-grid mw-grid-cards mw-grid-cols-3

docs.title: Block Grids
docs.text:
A [grid ...] paired with [/grid] is a block grid. It wraps everything between its lines in a <div class="mw-grid">, and each child block is a grid cell. The opener takes the same cards and count tokens as the shortcut, so a block grid can be [grid cards 2] ... [/grid].

A block grid holds any Markdown block, from a heading to a list.

Each top-level block between the opener and the closer is one cell.

Markdown 
[grid 2]

A block grid holds any Markdown block, from a heading to a list.

Each top-level block between the opener and the closer is one cell.

[/grid]

An unclosed [grid ...] falls back to the list shortcut. A list shortcut cannot sit directly inside a block grid at the same indentation: the block grid's [/grid] pairs with the nearer inner opener, turning that inner opener into a block grid and leaving the outer [grid] unclosed, so the outer grid demotes to a shortcut. To nest a shortcut list, put it inside a [card], whose [/card] leaves the unclosed [grid ...] intact as a shortcut, or close the inner grid to get a nested block grid instead.

docs.title: Cards
docs.text:
A [card] paired with [/card] directly inside a block grid wraps its content in <div class="mw-card">. One card holds several blocks, such as a heading, a paragraph, a list, and a link.

A [card] outside a block grid, an unclosed [card], and a stray [/card] stay literal text; see Fail-Soft and Warnings.

Markdown 
[grid cards 2]

[card]

### Pre Stage

`mw pre` expands the source to markers.

[/card]

[card]

### Post Stage

`mw post` applies the markers to the rendered HTML.

[/card]

[/grid]

docs.title: Nesting
docs.text:
Containers nest freely: a card in a grid, a grid in a card, a grid in a grid. A nested opener and its closer sit at the same indentation as each other.

Markdown 
[grid 2]

[card]

### Outer

[grid 2]

Nested cell one.

Nested cell two.

[/grid]

[/card]

[/grid]

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Grid is a two-stage extension. The source stage (mw pre) replaces each directive with a marker comment:

<!-- mw-grid:{"version": 1, "cards": true, "columns": 3} -->
<!-- mw-grid-block:{"version": 1, "cards": true, "columns": 3} -->
<!-- mw-grid-end:{"version": 1} -->
<!-- mw-card:{"version": 1} -->
<!-- mw-card-end:{"version": 1} -->

The HTML stage (mw post) classes the list a shortcut marker precedes, wraps the span between each block-grid or card open and close marker in a <div>, and removes every marker. It orders the open and close markers of a kind by position and matches them like brackets, so nested grids and cards wrap in order and close in reverse.

docs.title: HTML Contract
docs.text:
A list shortcut classes the list in place:

<ul class="mw-grid mw-grid-cards mw-grid-cols-3">
<li>One</li>
<li>Two</li>
</ul>

A block grid wraps its blocks, and each card wraps its own:

<div class="mw-grid mw-grid-cards mw-grid-cols-3">
<div class="mw-card">
<h3>Pre Stage</h3>
<p>Expands the source to markers.</p>
</div>
</div>

The mw-grid, mw-grid-cards, mw-grid-cols-N, and mw-card classes are the public contract. The cards class is mw-grid-cards.

docs.title: Marker Contracts
docs.text:
Each marker is a versioned public contract, read fail-soft like the fence marker.

Marker Payload Role mw-grid version, cards, columns Classes the list shortcut that follows it. mw-grid-block / mw-grid-end version, cards, columns on the opener Wrap a block grid in a <div>. mw-card / mw-card-end version Wrap a card in a <div class="mw-card">. mw-grid-problem version, line, directive, reason Mark a container left literal so mw post --warn reports it.

The cards and columns fields are present only when the opener carries them. A payload bumps its version with no migration shim when a field changes, since the project is pre-1.0 with one host.

docs.title: Escaping a Directive
docs.text: A backslash before the opening bracket keeps a standalone directive line literal: \[grid 3], \[card], \[/grid], and \[/card]. Markdown's own escape removes the backslash, so the line renders as the text [grid 3] with no grid, no marker, and no report. It works the same in-process and through mw pre | renderer | mw post.

docs.title: Fail-Soft and Warnings
docs.text:
A directive the extension cannot turn into markup stays literal and is reported by mw post --warn, never raised:

  • an unclosed [card];
  • a stray [/card] or [/grid];
  • a [card] whose nearest enclosing container is not a block grid.

The pre stage attaches an inline mw-grid-problem marker to each literal directive, and the post stage composes one --warn line from the marker and removes the comment. An invalid [grid ...] is not an opener, so its own line stays literal with no report; its [/grid] is a stray closer and is reported, and a [card] under it is outside a grid and is reported once. An opener or closer inside fenced or indented code also stays literal, with no report. A shortcut marker is skipped, and --warn reports why, when its payload is invalid or no list follows it.

docs.title: Host CSS and Script
docs.text:
markwright ships no CSS, JavaScript, or icons. The hooks are the mw-grid wrapper, the mw-grid-cards class on a cards grid, the mw-grid-cols-N column count, and the mw-card class on each card; they are inert until the host styles them, and no host script is involved. This site's grid rules in docs/stylesheets/extra.css follow mkdocs-material's:

  • .mw-grid is a CSS grid that flows items into as many columns as fit and drops to one on a narrow screen; mw-grid-cols-N pins an exact count.
  • .mw-card and a cards list's items get a hairline border that lifts into a shadow on hover or focus.
  • A card's opening icon is drawn at twice the text size, centered on the title.

docs.title: Highlight
docs.text:
Converts <^>text<^> to <mark>text</mark>. Works in regular text, inline code, and fenced code blocks, anywhere that pymdownx.mark (==text==) cannot reach.

Set config.timeout to 30 seconds before you deploy:

config.timeout = 30
Markdown 
Set `config.<^>timeout<^>` to <^>30 seconds<^> before you deploy:

```python
config.timeout = <^>30<^>
```

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import markdown

md = markdown.Markdown(extensions=["markwright.highlight"])
html = md.convert("This has a <^>highlighted word<^> in it.")

See Using with MkDocs to load it in a MkDocs site.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Wrap text in <^> delimiters:

This has a <^>highlighted word<^> in it.

Result: This has a highlighted word in it.

docs.title: In Inline Code
docs.text:
Check the `config.<^>timeout<^>` value.

Result: Check the config.timeout value.

docs.title: In Fenced Code Blocks
docs.text:
```python
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, <^>{name}<^>!")
```

Result:

def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

docs.title: Multiple Highlights
docs.text:
Multiple highlights work on the same line:

Both <^>first<^> and <^>second<^> are highlighted.

Result: Both first and second are highlighted.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
In text, a marker pairs with the next marker on the same line, so a highlight never holds a line end. A marker with no partner on its line stays as written. A pair may hold an inline code span, which the highlight covers whole; a marker inside the code span is not part of the pair.

Set <^>the `timeout` value<^> first.

Result: Set the timeout value first.

docs.title: Escaping
docs.text:
Prefix a marker with a backslash (<^>) to show it literally instead of applying a highlight. This works consistently in regular text, inline code, and fenced code blocks, and produces the same literal marker whether you render in-process or through the mw pre | post pipeline. This is how the code samples above print the raw <^> syntax.

In text, backslashes before a marker are read in pairs: two of them print one backslash and leave the marker live, three print one backslash and a literal marker. A literal marker is written <^> in the HTML, so running mw post again leaves it alone.

docs.title: HTML Contract
docs.text:
Prose and inline code get a <mark> element:

<p>A <mark>word</mark> here and <code>a.<mark>b</mark></code></p>

Inside a fenced code block the <mark> wraps the highlighted text, and the post stage places it so it never crosses a syntax-highlighting <span>. <mark> is the whole contract.

docs.title: Host CSS and Script
docs.text: markwright ships no CSS, JavaScript, or icons. The only hook is the <mark> element, which browsers already draw with a default highlight, so highlights show with no host code. This site restyles <mark> to match mkdocs-material, both in prose and inside a syntax-highlighted block, under the .md-typeset mark and .md-typeset .highlight mark rules in docs/stylesheets/extra.css. A host that wants a different highlight color overrides those rules; no script is needed.

docs.title: Icons
docs.text:
Replaces :pack-name: shortcodes in prose with inline SVG read from directories you configure.

markwright ships no icons. You name a pack (a prefix) and point it at a directory of SVG files, and the extension inlines the file whose name matches.

Build passed

Rated by readers who it.

Next step install, then run.

Markdown 
Build passed :lucide-check:

Rated :mw-star: :mw-star: :mw-star: by readers who :mw-heart: it.

Next step :lucide-arrow-right: install, then :mw-bolt: run.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import markdown

md = markdown.Markdown(
    extensions=["markwright.icons"],
    extension_configs={
        "markwright.icons": {
            "packs": {
                "lucide": "docs/icons/lucide",
                "mw": "docs/icons/mw",
            },
        },
    },
)

See Using with MkDocs to load it in a MkDocs site.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Description packs omitted (no packs) A table of pack prefix to the directory holding that pack's SVG files.

The same option works in markwright.toml:

[icons.packs]
lucide = "docs/icons/lucide"
mw = "docs/icons/mw"

Relative directories resolve against the directory you run from. With no packs, the extension does nothing and shortcodes stay text. An empty packs table emits a ConfigWarning, and a non-table value, a non-string path, or a directory that does not exist is a ConfigError. See Configuration.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
:PACK-NAME:

The shortcode is the pack prefix, a hyphen, and the icon name. :lucide-check: reads check.svg from the lucide pack's directory. A file in a subdirectory joins its path parts with hyphens, so arrows/up.svg is the name arrows-up. Prefixes are matched longest first.

A shortcode that names no pack, or a pack with no matching file, is left as text. Shortcodes inside fenced code blocks and inline code spans are never replaced, and mw pre leaves a diagram that the mermaid stage converted alone. It reads a <pre class="mermaid"> block you write yourself the same way, through the first </pre>, so a shortcode inside it stays literal text. In mw pre the icons stage runs after every directive stage, so a shortcode inside a [button] line is read as part of the directive, and a shortcode in a [tab] name stays literal text. Anything before the <svg tag in the file (an XML declaration or a license comment) is dropped, and the markup is joined onto a single line.

An unknown icon stays text: :lucide-nope: and :lucide-nope:.

docs.title: HTML Contract
docs.text:
<span aria-hidden="true" class="mw-icon"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg></span>

The wrapper is a span with class="mw-icon" and aria-hidden="true", in that serialized order, so icons are decorative to screen readers. The SVG inside is the file's own markup, unchanged.

docs.title: Host CSS and Script
docs.text:
markwright ships no CSS, JavaScript, or icons. The only hook is the span.mw-icon wrapper, which carries aria-hidden="true" and holds the pack's own SVG; no host script is involved. The demo packs on this site are committed under docs/icons/. lucide holds check, arrow-right, and info (ISC license), and mw holds star, heart, and bolt, drawn for this repository. Credits and license text are in docs/icons/CREDITS.txt.

Sizing and color are the host's job, and the .mw-icon rules in docs/stylesheets/extra.css show one way. Icons that use currentColor, as both demo packs do, take the surrounding text color.

docs.title: Image Compare
docs.text:
Creates side-by-side image comparisons with an interactive slider control.

Markdown 
[compare https://picsum.photos/id/10/480/270 https://picsum.photos/id/20/480/270]

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import markdown

md = markdown.Markdown(extensions=["markwright.image_compare"])
html = md.convert("[compare https://example.com/before.jpg https://example.com/after.jpg]")

See Using with MkDocs to load it in a MkDocs site.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
[compare URL1 URL2 HEIGHT WIDTH]
Parameter Default Description URL1 required Left image URL URL2 required Right image URL HEIGHT 270 Widget height in pixels WIDTH 480 Widget width in pixels

docs.title: Custom Dimensions
docs.text: [compare https://picsum.photos/id/10/600/400 https://picsum.photos/id/20/600/400 400 600]

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The embed must be on its own line, with a blank line before and after it; without them the renderer folds the embed into the surrounding paragraph
  • Exactly 2 image URLs are required (no more, no fewer)
  • The slider starts at 50% and uses a CSS custom property (--value) for positioning
  • No script injection required; uses an inline oninput handler

docs.title: HTML Contract
docs.text:
<div class="image-compare" style="--value:50%; height: 270px; width: 480px;">
    <img class="image-left" src="https://picsum.photos/id/10/480/270" alt="Image left"/>
    <img class="image-right" src="https://picsum.photos/id/20/480/270" alt="Image right"/>
    <input type="range" class="control" min="0" max="100" value="50"
      oninput="this.parentNode.style.setProperty('--value', `${this.value}%`)" />
    <svg class="control-arrow" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 512 512"><path fill="currentColor" d="..."/></svg>
</div>

The <path> data is shortened here.

docs.title: Host CSS and Script
docs.text: markwright ships no CSS, JavaScript, or icons. The hooks are the image-compare wrapper (do-markdownit's own shape), its image-left and image-right images, and the control range input with its control-arrow; the slider position rides a --value custom property that an inline oninput handler updates, so the comparison works with no host script. This site sizes and clips the two images and styles the slider in the .image-compare rules of docs/stylesheets/extra.css; without that CSS markwright emits only the structure, so the host CSS is what makes the overlay visible.

graph LR
  Source[Markdown source] --> Pre[mw pre]
  Pre --> Renderer
  Renderer --> Post[mw post]
  Post --> HTML
Markdown 
```mermaid
graph LR
  Source[Markdown source] --> Pre[mw pre]
  Pre --> Renderer
  Renderer --> Post[mw post]
  Post --> HTML
```

md = markdown.Markdown(extensions=["markwright.mermaid"])

See Using with MkDocs to load it in a MkDocs site.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Tag a fence with mermaid and write the diagram inside:

```mermaid
graph LR
  A[Source] --> B[Rendered HTML]
```

Only a closed fence whose info string is exactly mermaid is converted. An unclosed fence is not a code block, so it is left alone. Other fences, and a mermaid fence shown inside a longer outer fence like the one above, pass through unchanged.

docs.title: HTML Contract
docs.text:
<pre class="mermaid">graph LR
  A[Source] --> B[Rendered HTML]
</pre>

This site does it in docs/javascripts/mermaid.js, which imports a pinned Mermaid build from a CDN and calls mermaid.initialize({ startOnLoad: true }). docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
Groups content into a tab set. Each [tab NAME] paired with [/tab] is one tab, and consecutive tabs join one set with the first tab selected.

Python CLI

Call the extensions in-process with Python-Markdown, the same way the other extensions load.

Run the same stages as a shell filter with mw pre and mw post, so the syntax works around any renderer.

Markdown 
[tab Python]

Call the extensions in-process with Python-Markdown, the same way the other extensions load.

[/tab]

[tab CLI]

Run the same stages as a shell filter with `mw pre` and `mw post`, so the syntax works around any renderer.

[/tab]

The directive lines are inside the source fence above, so the pre stage leaves them literal and the fence renders the source as written.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import markdown

md = markdown.Markdown(extensions=["markwright.tabs"])

See Using with MkDocs to load it in a MkDocs site. Tabs reuses pymdown-extensions' tabbed classes, so a host theme that already styles tab sets styles these too, with no extra configuration and no dependency on pymdownx.tabbed.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Put each tab between a [tab NAME] opener and a [/tab] closer, each alone on its line:

Markdown 
[tab First]

Any Markdown goes here.

[/tab]

[tab Second]

So does the content of the next tab.

[/tab]
  • NAME is the rest of the opener line, trimmed. It is non-empty, holds no ], and may hold spaces, so [tab Node.js 20] is one tab named Node.js 20.
  • The name renders as escaped plain text; inline Markdown in it is not rendered.
  • Tabs separated only by blank lines group into one set.
  • Any other content between two tabs starts a new set, and the first tab in each set is selected.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Tabs is a two-stage extension. The source stage (mw pre) replaces each tab with an open and a close marker comment:

<!-- mw-tab:{"version": 1, "name": "Python", "first": true} -->
<!-- mw-tab-end:{"version": 1} -->

The first field is true for the tab that starts a set. The HTML stage (mw post) orders the markers by position, matches them like brackets, groups the tabs into sets at each first marker, and wraps each set in the tabbed markup. Every marker comment is removed.

docs.title: HTML Contract
docs.text:
A set renders as pymdown-extensions' tabbed alternate_style markup:

<div class="tabbed-set tabbed-alternate mw-tabs" data-tabs="1:2">
<input checked="checked" type="radio" id="mw-tab-1-1" name="mw-tab-1" />
<input type="radio" id="mw-tab-1-2" name="mw-tab-1" />
<div class="tabbed-labels">
<label for="mw-tab-1-1">Python</label>
<label for="mw-tab-1-2">CLI</label>
</div>
<div class="tabbed-content">
<div class="tabbed-block">
<p>The first tab's body.</p>
</div>
<div class="tabbed-block">
<p>The second tab's body.</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>

One radio <input> per tab shares the set's name="mw-tab-S", so checking one unchecks the rest, and the first is checked. S counts sets and T counts tabs within a set, both from 1 per document, so the ids run mw-tab-S-T. The mw-tab- prefix keeps the ids from colliding with pymdown-extensions' own __tabbed_ ids when a host loads both. data-tabs="S:N" records the set number and its tab count.

docs.title: Marker Contracts
docs.text:
Each marker is a versioned public contract, read fail-soft.

Marker Payload Role mw-tab / mw-tab-end version, name, first on the opener Wrap one tab, grouped into sets at each first. mw-tab-problem version, line, directive, reason Mark a tab left literal so mw post --warn reports it.

A payload bumps its version with no migration shim when a field changes, since the project is pre-1.0 with one host.

docs.title: Escaping a Directive
docs.text: A backslash before the opening bracket keeps a standalone directive line literal: \[tab Name] and \[/tab]. Markdown's own escape removes the backslash, so the line renders as the text [tab Name] with no tab, no marker, and no report. It works the same in-process and through mw pre | renderer | mw post.

docs.title: Fail-Soft and Warnings
docs.text:
A tab the extension cannot pair stays literal and is reported by mw post --warn, never raised:

  • an unclosed [tab NAME];
  • a stray [/tab].

The pre stage attaches an inline mw-tab-problem marker to each literal directive, and the post stage composes one --warn line from the marker and removes the comment. An empty [tab ] with no name is not an opener and stays literal with no report. An opener or closer inside fenced or indented code also stays literal.

docs.title: Host CSS and Script
docs.text: markwright ships no CSS, JavaScript, or icons. The tabbed-set, tabbed-alternate, tabbed-labels, tabbed-content, and tabbed-block classes are pymdown-extensions' own, reused so a host's existing tab CSS applies; the mw-tabs class, the mw-tab-S-T ids, and the mw-tab-S radio names are markwright's. Together they are the public contract, inert until the host styles them. This site's sample in docs/stylesheets/extra.css ties each radio's :checked state to the block at its position, so the demo above switches tabs with no JavaScript. The sample's :nth-child chains stop at six tabs, so a set's seventh tab and beyond would not switch under it; a host that needs more extends those chains, and a host with JavaScript or an existing .tabbed-set style has no such ceiling.
